en: They cut its plane trees and felled them.
Pulling out its pillars, the mosque
They flooded with water and brought down.
All its lattice walls
They demolished on every side.
Making war on the mosque,
They left it desolate.
The mosque had fallen and faded away.
When Semetey went and looked,
His father's great mosque—
Had crumbled into fragments.
Pools of spring water surrounded it.
The whole mosque had collapsed.
God had struck it down.
“My khan father's great mosque,
Shattered beyond recognition,
Has become the mound of Tort-Kul.
My fierce-maned father has died.
Not only my father's living wife—
Even his mosque has been smashed.
Thus they have brought it to ruin.
Not only my father's child—
They made war on his garden.
Alas, they cut it all down.
Its birds cried out.
All its plane trees had been cut down;
All its towers stood desolate.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six wicked ones—
God has struck down my uncles.
My leopard father, the bloodthirsty one—
They made war on the possessions he left,
Burning, crushing, destroying them,
Leaving them like an extinguished fire.
Thus God has dealt an extraordinary blow.”
Seeing the mosque, his heart burned.
His heart blazed and turned to embers;
Both his eyes became fire.
His thoughts were scattered and torn.
Like a man stricken with jaundice,
The boy shed tears from his eyes.
Allah's sun clouded over in the sky.
Upon your orphan's head
Sixty sorrows came at once.
Unable to collect himself,
The wretched orphan in distress
Went farther and grew distraught.
At the gray cliff west of Talas
The boy arrived.
“My precious mother had told me:
‘In this cliff, in safekeeping,
I hid your treasure,’ she said.
My poor leopard mother's
Treasure let me see.
Thus let me attain my desire.
The five strongmen who died innocent—
Let me recite the Qur'an for those poor men.
Let me see every sign.
Let me make ample offerings for those poor men.”
So said Semetey.
My poor mother Kanykei,
Telling her tale from long ago,
Crying bitterly to the one God,
Grieving for wretched me, calling me her orphan,
In her own lonely person,
My noble mother Kanykei
Had lost her bloodthirsty one
At only thirty-two years of age.
When the moon was dark,
“What will become of the night?” she said.
“The treasure left by precious Manas,
If I do not hide it for the orphan,
What will become of the day?” she said.
“Tomorrow, when the orphan grows up,
Matures and becomes a warrior,
Stands equal with other warriors' sons,
Comes to Talas and finds his land,
Comes to the Kyrgyz and finds his people,
Gathers what was scattered,
‘The vast wealth left by my father Manas—
Mother, where has it gone?’
If he asks wretched me,
What deep torment I shall suffer!
To the orphan left by the Magnanimous One,
What answer shall I give?
Tomorrow, when the orphan comes,
When he sees this Talas,
He will be left powerless,” she said.
“With no treasure at all,
My cherished orphan
Will be left without livestock,” she said.
Thinking wisely, considering what to do,
My resourceful mother Kanykei,
That poor woman, a true saint—
My father Manas had died.
With little me beneath her arm,
My mourning mother had remained.
From the Argyns and Kyrgyz
My valiant mother Kanykei
Chose five strongmen.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six wicked ones,
Would ravage his palace,
Would utterly destroy her—
My mother knew beforehand.
“They will all be my ruin,” she said.
“They will plunder my treasury,” she said.
“Then these men will wreak havoc,” she said.
My mother, knowing the news,
Without showing anyone,
Without letting anyone know,
Shouted in her wrath.
My ill-fated leopard mother
Summoned the five strongmen.
If they worked by day,
She gave a horse for a day's work.
If they worked by night,
For their night's work
She promptly gave a gold ingot.
She gave them tea to drink.
For the strongmen's food,
She gave fat lamb and choice heads,
And nothing but cooked fat.
Having steel mattocks found,
My incomparable mother
Had the face of the gray cliff excavated.
Having it broken open with iron crowbars,
Leaving it by day, digging by night,
Digging while eating her provisions,
Red gold and much property—
My mother Kanykei, blessed by Kydyr,
Had it dug to hide them.
Marking it out, she had an entrance hollowed,
Large enough for one person to enter.
She had the farther space hollowed out,
Large enough for six thousand sheep to lie down.
When the strongmen hollowed the cave,
My khan father's abundant gold—
When the time to hide it drew near,
Surpassing everyone in wisdom,
The sand and stones removed from within
She cleverly contrived to conceal.
From my khan father's many camels
She had seventy gelded camels saddled for loads.
She had the sand collected in sacks.
So that no one would find out,
Into the flowing Talas,
The sand from inside
She had poured into its great waters.
On Thursday,
My valiant mother Kanykei
Turned her attention to the wealth.
On Friday's holy night,
Her precious hair, long and thick,
Her poor self in mourning,
My mother could not stand idly by.
Unashamed of her wounded state,
She had the cave mouth prepared.
She had eighty gelded camels saddled for loads.
She had them work with great zeal.
The many gold coins left by my father Manas
Into the excavated cave
She had gathered in heaps.
Bukhara's heavy black-mottled cloth—
She had all of it bundled,
Saying, “This orphan will need it.”
My mother had it mingled together
And placed in the treasury.
Father, my valiant mother Kanykei
Had the gold gathered securely.
At the cave's mouth
She had the stonework fitted.
“If I abandon it, it will bring disgrace.
My beloved cave,
This was my orphan's wealth;
I entrust it to the One God!”
So saying, my mother
Had drawn the boundary line.
In the cave she made a treasury,
My mother had done a wondrous thing.
Black sand upon its roof,
So that it might remain unmarked,
My valiant mother Kanykei
Had broken up with iron crowbars
And brought down toward the cave's mouth.
My poor mother Kanykei
Thought and cried out,
Her worries scattered a thousand ways.
My poor mother sobbed:
“O God, I am left Manas's widow!
If I carry my only child away
And depart from Talas,
The warriors who have seen my cave,
Who have entered my dreams three times—
Will they turn hostile
To this deed I have done?
Will they turn informers among men
And together bring me to ruin?
Will those wretches suddenly
Break into my treasury?
Will they open the mouth of my store?
Will they scatter my wealth?
Will they ravage my possessions
And thus bring me to my end?”
My poor mother Kanykei
Harbored dark suspicions of the warriors.
My poor mother did not trust
Those people standing there.
Roaring in anger,
Those five innocent warriors
She tricked and called into the house.
As dusk fell and the sun set,
As the first of the people lay quiet,
To those five poor warriors
She gave water poured in a spoon,
Poison measured in a ladle.
Thinking deeply, acting with menace,
My valiant mother Kanykei
Removed the five warriors from this world.
Thus she had them eat her portion,
Made them all cry, “My liver!”
Grasped their steel and blunted it.
Because of me, the orphan,
My valiant mother Kanykei
Then destroyed those five warriors.
At the edge of the hearth,
Beneath the stone pot-rest,
She dug and hollowed out a pit.
Her crime: my mother slew five innocent men.
Grasping them, bent at the waist,
Beneath the hearth
She buried them without an outward trace.
There is more to tell of it:
She killed them though they had no crime.
When she comes to Judgment Day,
Upon my valiant mother's neck
Is the blood of five warriors.
There is no end to the tale,
Of my luckless mother, worn with anguish.
If the rumor people tell is true,
My poor mother Kanykei,
When she comes to Judgment Day,
May become a black donkey.
Does not the mortal's borrowed life end?
Allah has written it thus;
Must not the wretched mortal submit?”
Saying this then,
To Allah alone, whose command prevails,
He offered fervent supplication.
He readied and saddled the white steed.
His father's son, the noble lion,
For the five warriors
Recited the Quran with great care:
“If I reach Talas safely,
Five warriors of noble spirits,
I shall raise a palace above you,
Gather the poor beside you.
If my strength and skill suffice,
